rows.claim: The November 1330 parliament roll records Thomas de Berkeley answering for the death of Edward II, saying he never consented to, helped or procured the death, and never knew of it until that parliament.
rows.allowed_scope: The parliament roll records Lord Berkeley saying he never consented to the death, and never knew of it until that parliament.
rows.sources: *Rotuli Parliamentorum* ii (1767), p. 57, Pleas of the Crown, Westminster, Monday after St Katherine (26 Nov 1330), 4 Edw III; raw/10213330bsb_djvu.txt. Latin as printed: "Dicit, quod ipfe nuncquam fuit confentiens, auxi-" ... "de morte fua ufq; in prefenti Parliamento ifto. Et de". Same roll: he says that at the time he was ill "apud Bradeleye" outside the castle.
quotes: Dicit, quod ipfe nuncquam fuit confentiens, auxi-
de morte fua ufq; in prefenti Parliamento ifto. Et de
nor did he ever know of his death until this present parliament
rows.permitted_wording: The parliament roll records Lord Berkeley saying he never consented to the death, and never knew of it until that parliament.
rows.seen: FIRST-HAND (printed roll). PROME text and translation: GAP (premium, raw/bho-prome-nov1330.txt). PROME English seen SECOND-HAND via Warner 2013: "nor did he ever know of his death until this present parliament".

rows.claim: Responsible English (my translation of the printed Latin, for desk use): He says that he was never consenting, helping or procuring to his death, nor did he ever know of his death until this present parliament.
rows.allowed_scope: Use the translation above, labelled as the parliament roll; do not credit PROME on screen until someone checks PROME directly.
rows.sources: as C01a
rows.permitted_wording: Use the translation above, labelled as the parliament roll; do not credit PROME on screen until someone checks PROME directly.
rows.seen: FIRST-HAND (my rendering, checked against the PROME wording quoted by Warner and by Carpenter's LRB rendering)

rows.claim: What Berkeley meant. Ian Mortimer reads it as Berkeley denying that the king died; Carpenter reads it as Berkeley denying knowledge of a murder.
rows.allowed_scope: Historians disagree about what he meant.
rows.sources: Carpenter, LRB 29/11 (7 Jun 2007) and LRB 29/15 letters (2 Aug 2007): "Ian Mortimer persists in quoting only the second half of Lord Berkeley's statement"; Mortimer, LRB 29/13 letters (5 Jul 2007). Warner blog Sept 2013 cites Haines 2002 p. 78, Phillips 2010 pp. 579 to 580 n. 18, D.J.H. Smith (TLS, GAP).
quotes: Ian Mortimer persists in quoting only the second half of Lord Berkeley's statement
rows.permitted_wording: Historians disagree about what he meant.
rows.seen: Carpenter and Mortimer letters FIRST-HAND (raw/lrb-carpenter-2007-what-happened.txt). Haines, Phillips, Smith SECOND-HAND via Warner.

rows.claim: A letter of Archbishop William Melton of York, dated 14 January, to Simon Swanland, mayor of London, reports news that Edward of Caernarfon was alive and well, and concerns money and clothing for him. The original survives in the Newdegate family archive (Arbury Hall), now Warwickshire County Record Office CR 136/C/2027.
rows.allowed_scope: A letter from the archbishop of York, which still survives, reported news that the former king was alive.
rows.required_attribution: A letter from the archbishop of York, which still survives, reported news that the former king was alive.
rows.sources: Edition: R.M. Haines, 'Sumptuous Apparel for a Royal Prisoner: Archbishop Melton's Letter, 14 January 1330', EHR 124 (2009) 885 to 894, doi 10.1093/ehr/cep186 (GAP, closed access). Haines abstract (OpenAlex): "an original letter sent by the archbishop of York, William Melton, to Simon Swonlond, the mayor of London" and "Printed for the first time". Shelfmark CR 136/C/2027 via Mortimer S3.
quotes: an original letter sent by the archbishop of York, William Melton, to Simon Swonlond, the mayor of London
nous avoms certeins noueles de nostre seignur lige Edward de Karnarvan qil est en vie
rows.permitted_wording: A letter from the archbishop of York, which still survives, reported news that the former king was alive.
rows.seen: Letter text SECOND-HAND only. Warner's blog quotes the French "nous avoms certeins noueles de nostre seignur lige Edward de Karnarvan qil est en vie" (not checked against Haines). Original not seen; not in TNA Discovery.

rows.claim: Year of the Melton letter.
rows.allowed_scope: Its modern editor dates it to January 1330, and the mayor's term of office supports that. Or: early 1330. Never state the year as bare fact; never say months before Kent's arrest unattributed.
rows.sources: Haines's title gives 1330. Warner: "almost certainly in 1330 (though 1329 is also possible)". TNA C 241 recognisances (raw/tna-discovery-simon-swanland-2026-10-30.txt) taken "Before whom: Simon de Swanland, Mayor of London" run from "When taken: 01/10/1329" to "When taken: 16/10/1330", with none earlier in the capture. A letter of 14 January addressed to him as mayor therefore fits January 1330, not January 1329 (v2: our reading of the catalogue, consistent with Haines).
quotes: almost certainly in 1330 (though 1329 is also possible)
Before whom: Simon de Swanland, Mayor of London
rows.permitted_wording: Its modern editor dates it to January 1330, and the mayor's term of office supports that. Or: early 1330. Never state the year as bare fact; never say months before Kent's arrest unattributed.
rows.seen: Haines, Warner SECOND-HAND; mayoral dates FIRST-HAND in TNA catalogue; the inference from them is ours

rows.claim: Fieschi's letter, as printed from the Maguelone cartulary, gives this itinerary in this order: Chepstow; by boat to Glamorgan, captured; Kenilworth, loses the crown; his son crowned at Candlemas; Berkeley; escape in a servant's clothes; Corfe for a year and a half; hears that Kent was beheaded for saying he lived; Ireland; back to England as a hermit, landing at Sandwich; over the sea at Sluys; Normandy; through Languedoc to Avignon, kept by Pope John more than fifteen days; Paris; Brabant; Cologne, to see the Three Kings; across Germany to Milan; a hermitage of the castle Milasci for two and a half years; war; to the castle Cecinie, another hermitage in the diocese of Pavia, about two years.
rows.allowed_scope: Fieschi's letter claims the former king escaped Berkeley, hid at Corfe, then wandered through Ireland, the Low Countries, Avignon and Germany to hermitages in Lombardy. Always framed as the letter's claim.
rows.sources: Germain, 'Lettre de Manuel de Fiesque', Mém. Soc. archéol. Montpellier VII, pp. (118) to (120), from "Cartul. de Mag., Reg. À, fol. 86, r°.)"; raw/memoiressociarcheomontpel7_djvu.txt. Key strings: "In nomine Domini. Amen. Ea que audivi ex confessione patris vestri, manu propria"; "quod vocatur Gesosta."; "Ultimum miserunt eum ad castrum de Berchelee."; "fuit receptatus in castro de Corf"; "secrete fuit per annum cum dimidio"; "audito quod comes Cancii, quia dixerat"; "transivit in Yrlandam"; "aplicuit ad portum de Sandvic"; "transivit mare apud Sclusam"; "venit Avinionem"; "peresit Mediolanum in Lombardiam"; "mutavit se in castro Cecinie, in alio heremitorio"; "diocesis Papiensis"; signed "Vester Manuel de Flisco, domini Pape notarius, devotus servitor vester." Reprinted by Stubbs 1883 (RS 76 ii, intro pp. civ to cvi), raw/stubbs-chronicles-edw-i-ii-vol2-1883_djvu.txt. One passage about Berkeley omitted here under the no-gore rule.
quotes: Cartul. de Mag., Reg. À, fol. 86, r°.)
In nomine Domini. Amen. Ea que audivi ex confessione patris vestri, manu propria
Ultimum miserunt eum ad castrum de Berchelee.
fuit receptatus in castro de Corf
secrete fuit per annum cum dimidio
audito quod comes Cancii, quia dixerat
mutavit se in castro Cecinie, in alio heremitorio
Vester Manuel de Flisco, domini Pape notarius, devotus servitor vester.
rows.permitted_wording: Fieschi's letter claims the former king escaped Berkeley, hid at Corfe, then wandered through Ireland, the Low Countries, Avignon and Germany to hermitages in Lombardy. Always framed as the letter's claim.
rows.seen: FIRST-HAND (two independent 19th c. prints; Germain page image checked, raw/germain-1878-p119-IMAGE-CHECK.txt). Manuscript not seen. Tout 1920 summarises only (not a reprint).

rows.allowed_scope: Some months in Ireland. Prefer no number; if one is unavoidable, eight or nine months depending on the edition. Never quote the OCR form vint.

date of the MS. is about A.D. 1400.

rows.claim: The Brut says Kent asked Pope John XXII at Avignon for counsel, telling him of a common report throughout England that Edward was alive; the pope charged him on his blessing to help. On Kent's return, friars preachers said Edward was alive at Corfe. Kent went to Corfe himself, befriended Sir John Deveril and gave him a letter for Edward; Deveril took the sealed letter to Roger Mortimer. Kent's confession separately says the pope charged him to work for his brother's deliverance, and that he sent letters to Deveril under his seal. (v2: v1 said Kent heard at Avignon; the Brut has Kent bring the report to the pope. Corfe visit added from p. 264. The friar's claim moved to C09b.)
rows.allowed_scope: According to the Brut, Kent went to the pope at Avignon and spoke of a common report in England that Edward was alive; friars later told him Edward was at Corfe; he went there himself and gave a sealed letter for Edward to Deveril, who took it to Mortimer. Never say Kent first heard the news at Avignon. Do not name Deveril's office (the Brut calls him "conestable"; STANDING-LAW bars it). For Deveril's role prefer the record (C29).
rows.required_attribution: According to the Brut, Kent went to the pope at Avignon and spoke of a common report in England that Edward was alive; friars later told him Edward was at Corfe; he went there himself and gave a sealed letter for Edward to Deveril, who took it to Mortimer. rows.claim: Kent's widow Margaret, and separately his son Edmund, petitioned in the Westminster parliament (the morrow of St Nicholas, 7 Dec 1330) for the record of Kent's trial to be reviewed.
rows.allowed_scope: Within weeks of Mortimer's fall, Kent's widow asked parliament to reopen his case. (Mortimer's dying admission: CONTEMPORARY CLAIM, attribute to the petition.)
rows.sources: Rot. Parl. ii 55: "Margarete Counteffe de Kent" and "pur lui et pur" "fes Enfauntz". The petition also says Mortimer acknowledged at his death, before the people, that Kent died wrongfully.
rows.permitted_wording: Within weeks of Mortimer's fall, Kent's widow asked parliament to reopen his case. (Mortimer's dying admission: CONTEMPORARY CLAIM, attribute to the petition.)

rows.claim: Date of Fieschi's letter and its surviving form.

rows.permitted_wording: Probably written in the later 1330s; it survives as a copy made decades later.

rows.claim: The chronicler Murimuth says the plot rested on a falsehood, that confessions and letters found with Kent led to his death, and that he was less mourned because his household took people's goods as they travelled, paying little or nothing ("parum vel nihil solventes eisdem").
rows.allowed_scope: A contemporary chronicler called the whole story false, but thought Kent's death unjust.

rows.claim: Date of the death as announced, and when the news reached Edward III. Packet movement 3 says the death was announced on the night of 21 Sept. (v2: the announced date is disputed.)
rows.allowed_scope: Edward was said to have died in late September 1327; word reached the young king at Lincoln a couple of days later. Never narrate 21 or 22 Sept as the announced date: the official version (21 Sept, via secondary sources) and Murimuth (22 Sept) differ.
rows.sources: Murimuth p. 53: "Postea, x. kalendas Octobris" (22 Sept by the Roman count; my reading). Wikipedia, Edward II (raw/wikipedia-Edward_II.noref.txt, secondary): "On 23 September Edward III was informed that his father had died at Berkeley Castle during the night of 21 September." Carpenter: news received "on 23 September at Lincoln"; Masses yearly "on 21 September".
quotes: On 23 September Edward III was informed that his father had died at Berkeley Castle during the night of 21 September.
rows.permitted_wording: Edward was said to have died in late September 1327; word reached the young king at Lincoln a couple of days later. Never narrate 21 or 22 Sept as the announced date: the official version (21 Sept, via secondary sources) and Murimuth (22 Sept) differ.
rows.seen: Murimuth, Carpenter FIRST-HAND; government date SECOND-HAND

rows.permitted_wording: In 1326 the king fled west to Chepstow, was captured in South Wales, held at Kenilworth, and moved to Berkeley in spring 1327.
rows.seen: Roll and Stubbs FIRST-HAND; dates SECOND-HAND (Wikipedia)

rows.claim: The November 1330 parliament judged John Maltravers guilty of Kent's death, as the man who, knowing Edward was dead, made Kent believe he lived; the same judgment was given against Boeges de Bayons and John Deveril for the same cause, with rewards for their capture.

Parl. ii (raw/10213330bsb_djvu.txt, between the printed page markers 51 and 55; exact page not pinned from the OCR): "Qe Johan Mautravers fi eft cupable de la mort Efmon" "Counte de Kent"; "dit Johan favoit la niort le Roi Edward"; "de Boeges de Bayons, & Johan Deveroill, par la". rows.claim: Berkeley acquitted: at the octave of St Hilary (January 1331) a jury of twelve knights found Thomas de Berkeley not guilty of the death or of assent, aid or procurement, saying he was so ill at Bradley outside his castle that his life was despaired of. Because he had appointed Gurney and Ockley as keepers, by whom the king was murdered, he was given a day at the next parliament.

Parl. ii 57 (raw/10213330bsb_djvu.txt): "in ottabis Sci Hillarii"; "omnes Milites"; "nullo eft culpabilis de morte prediéti Domini Edwardi"; "Ideo idem Thomas inde quietus."; "Thomiam de Guriieyé, & Willm de Ocle, ad cuftodiam"; "Rex extitit murdratus". Berkeley and Maltravers each kept him a month at a time.
